core.text: When something is *so* big, *so* fast, *so* foolish *that* something follows, Latin uses **ut + subjunctive after tam / ita / tantus (the 'so … that' clause)**. A signal word — *tam* (so, before an adjective or adverb), *ita* or *sīc* (in such a way), *tantus* (so big), *tālis* (of such a kind), *tot* (so many) — is answered by *ut* and a verb in the subjunctive (the form Latin uses for wishes, purposes and what someone tells someone to do). Latin name: *coniūnctīvus cōnsecūtīvus*.
English: she was *so* tired *that* she fell asleep. The *so … that* pair is the whole idea; Latin only adds a special verb form in the *that* part.
Signal word (tam, ita, sīc, tantus, tālis, tot) + ut + subjunctive = result. The negative is ut nōn, not nē.

invented.la: Puer tam fessus erat ut statim dormīret.
invented.en: The boy was so tired that he fell asleep at once.

invented.la: Tanta erat tempestās ut nāvis nōn movērētur.
invented.en: The storm was so great that the ship did not move.

core.text: Purpose also uses *ut*, but has no signal word and its negative is *nē*. Test: can you add 'in order'? *vēnit ut vidēret* = came in order to see (purpose); *tam fessus erat ut dormīret* = so tired that he slept (result). *ut nōn* is always result.

more.text: The learner's notes sort the signal words by what is measured: *tam* for the degree of an adjective (*tam fortis est ut …*), *tantus* for the size of a thing, *tālis* for its kind, *ita* for the manner of an action (*ita clāmat ut audiātur*, he shouts so that he is heard), *tot* for a number. Sometimes the signal word is left out; then only sense decides — a purpose is intended but not necessarily achieved, a result is achieved but not necessarily intended.

The tense follows the sequence of tenses: *ita clāmō ut proximōs suscitem* (I shout so as to wake the neighbours) but *ita clāmāvī ut … suscitārem*. Ørberg's chapter 29: *Dāvus ita clāmat ut puerum excitet*; *Syra tam quiēta erat ut puellam nōn excitāret*.

Also easy to confuse: an indirect command, *ut* after a verb of ordering or asking (*imperat ut taceat*, orders him to be quiet) — no signal word, negative *nē*. And verbs meaning 'bring it about' take a result-style clause: *faciam* — I will see to it — *ut tergum eī doleat*, that his back hurts (Week 4).
